en: Thus, for a yogin who practices either the stage of generation (*utpattikrama*) or the stage of completion (*niṣpannakrama*), while he is dwelling [in this state], the Vajrayoginīs will necessarily reveal themselves by means of signs (*saṃketa*) for the purpose of meeting. Therefore, in order to explain those signs, he says: "O Blessed One," and so forth. This must indeed be understood even by others, lest they too might show [such signs] to them at some time. As for the secret sign of the mudrās, it is the indicative statement; its characteristic is that it is a secret to be concealed.

For the sake of the victory of the *yogins* and *yoginīs*, and for the sake of bringing them under one's own control through affection; that which possesses power (*bala*) is so described. *Samaya* means a meeting. For that purpose, he took the *mudrā*. Regarding "Kollagiri": at the sacred seat (*pīṭha*) of Kollagiri, there was the *yogin* known as Bola; at the field (*kṣetra*) of Mummuṇa, there was the *yoginī* known as Kakkolā.

Here, the instantaneous union of Wisdom and Means, though situated far apart, is described as occurring according to their respective natures like two sovereigns. *Kipiṭṭa* refers to the hand-drum (*ḍamaru*). *Ho* is an exclamation of address. *Karune* means "by means of compassion. *Kiaï na* means "are not performed. *Rolā* means quarrel. *Mayaṇā* means passion (*madana*). *Mālaï indhaṇa sālia* refers to rice as a condiment. *Bharu* means abundant. *Aṅgaṃ* means "in the limbs. *Caḍāviya* means having placed upon. *Tahi ja* means "and there. *Sarāva* means even resting.

*Paṇiaï* means "is introduced. By this much, there are four verses (*gāthās*). At the end of these, the *dhruvaka* (refrain) should be sung. He states that very thing with the words beginning with *malayajam*. Thus, the implicit meaning (*neyārtha*) is clear.

The definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), however, is as follows: Kollagiri is the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*); Mummuṇi is the emanation wheel (*nirmāṇacakra*). Therein, wisdom and method are said to be the *bola* and *kakkola*. Their resonance (*nāda*) is the sound of the *kṛpīṭa*. And in this regard, there is no quarrel between the Blessed One and Caṇḍālī, who has been stirred by the resonance of the syllable *Aṃ*; for the Blessed One is of the nature of the nectar of compassion (*karuṇāmṛta*). Rather, the Blessed One embraces her alone—the power (*bala*) residing in the heart-wheel and the other centers.

The burning and devouring by Caṇḍālī; the intoxication is the stream of bodhicitta. Kāliñjara is the downward-moving wind; its entry is into the avadhūtī. Durdura is the wind that has entered the lalanā and rasanā; its avoidance is the closing off of it therein. And the digestion and adherence of the four elixirs (catuḥsama) and so forth occurs when the limbs have been heated by the radiance of Caṇḍālī.

Then, after performing a fire offering as desired in the fire of the Caṇḍālī’s radiance, one should consume the digested four-fold elixir (*catuḥsama*)—which pervades all limbs—as well as the *śāli* rice, which serves as the condiment. Thereafter follows the swinging (*preṅkhaṇa*) and the chewing (*kheṭa*), the going to the place of the Blessed One, and returning with him to the Caṇḍālī. At that time, for the mind whose sole flavor is great bliss (*mahāsukha*), there is no arising of conceptual constructions regarding the auspicious or inauspicious, and no mental engagement with the pure or the impure.

When the channels have been purified by the radiance of Caṇḍālī, the moonbeams of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) fill them; this is the imposition of the partless [bliss] upon the limbs. Thus, for that which has become a corpse—the remaining body—there is the complete digestion (*jāraṇa*) within the radiance of the moon and sun, which is the entry into the corpse. This is the experience of the great bliss of equal flavor (*samarasa*), continuing as long as saṃsāra lasts, through wisdom and method (*prajñopāya*) which pervade all limbs, like the rubbing together of *malayaja* and *kunduru*.

And when such a state has arisen and all-encompassing transcendence (*abhyudgatatva*) has been attained, there is no longer the abandonment of the afflictions (*kleśa*) that are like drums; rather, it is the abandonment of those that are completely pure. For those whose essence is of one taste with that [transcendence], this is their very exaltation. And in this case of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), the previously mentioned interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*) serves as an auxiliary; likewise, the elaboration (*prapañca*) to be described hereafter is a limb of the means (*upāya*). Thus it was said before: "When the thirty-two types of bodhicitta reach fullness here..."

"Buddhahood [is attained] immediately after the elements have become the aggregates of the sense faculties. This does not mean that the state of Vajradhara is achieved by this alone; rather, one must practice according to the instructions for the sake of abandoning ordinary conceptualization and for the realization of the innate reality (*sahaja-tattva*). Therefore, the meaning is that the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā is then achieved without effort.

Having recited the song, he indicates the word-seal (*vākyamudrā*), beginning with "In the mouth," and so forth. This instruction is found in the twenty-fifth [chapter]. The limb-seal (*aṅgamudrā*) should be displayed by the yogin with his right hand, but by the yoginī with her left. Extending both hands in the form of a hollowed cup (*añjali*) and placing them at the mouth is the sign of the goddess Ḍākinī; *gho ghv* is the verbal convention. Holding the hollowed cup at the head is also the sign of Dīpinī; *gu ghv* is the verbal [convention].

Raising the hands in *añjali* with the middle fingers pressed together by the mouth is the sign of Cūṣiṇī; the word is "mu ghv. Striking both hands against the ears is the sign of Kambojī; the word is "lu ghv. Touching the tip of the nose and saying "draṣṭ" indicates two things: it suggests news of well-being and asks about one's welfare. Showing the five fingers like the head of a deer and saying "draṣṭ" indicates two things: [it signifies] an answer. A man is called "ḍā."

Each single syllable is used according to the context for the purpose of conventional terminology: *strī* (woman) is *ḍī*; *stambhanaṃ* (paralysis) is *pu*; *bhakṣaṇaṃ* (eating) is *su*; *mātā* (mother) is *mā*; *bhāryā* (wife) is *yo*; *bhaginī* (sister) is *bhi*; *sakhā* (friend) is *dhī*; *duhitā* (daughter) is *lu*; *rudhiraṃ* (blood) is *strī*; the drinking of *soma* or *śukra* (semen) is *sa*; the drink is *pe*; *māṃsaṃ* (flesh) is *phī*; eating is *bha*; the meeting place of the *yoginīs* is *bhū*; the cremation ground (*śmaśāna*) is *pī*; a corpse (*mṛtaka*) is *bhu*; the *yoginī* is *hī*; the *lāmā* families are *gā*; the *rūpiṇī* families are *tri*.

The classes of Ḍākinīs are *ku*; the classes of Khaṇḍarohā are *hā*. The two shanks are *ja*; the two arms are *ke*. Salutation is *bha*; words of welcome are *sva*. Pullīramalaya is *pu*; Jālandhara is *jā*; Oḍḍiyāṇa is *u*; Arbuda is *aḥ*. Godāvarī is *go*; Rāmeśvara is *rā*; Devīkoṭṭā is *de*; Mālava is *mā*; Kāmarūpa is *kā*; Oḍra is *o*; Triśakuni is *tri*; Kosala is *ko*; Kaliṅga is *ka*; Lampāka is *la*; Kāñcī is *kā*; Himālaya is *hi*.
Pretapurī is *pre*; Gṛhadevatā is *gṛ*; Saurāṣṭra is *sau*; Suvarṇadvīpa is *su*; Nagara is *na*; Sindhu is *si*; Maru is *ma*; Kulatā is *ku*.

To demonstrate another convention (*saṃketa*), he says: "Now," and so forth. *Chommā* refers to the secret signs (*milicchā*) of the yoginīs. A "brother" is a yogī; a "sister" is a yoginī. "Salutation" is *potaṅgī*; "return salutation" is *pratipotaṅgī*. "I go" is *gamu*; "I come" is *lumba*. "Give" is *nigara*; "take" is *caṭuka*. "Hero" is the heart; "killing" is *kauravā* and *kaurava*. "Bell" is *karṇikā*; "head" is *alikaraṇa*. "Hair" is *varāha*; "ear" is *śravaṇa*.

Amṛta is the churning-stick; *samāgama* is the man. *Ḍākinī* is the clapping of hands; *maṇḍala* is hell. (418v/840) The cremation ground is such-and-such; the door is *kākhilā*. The Brāhmaṇa is *svasana*; the Kṣatriya is the enclosure (*paridhi*). The Vaiśya is cessation (*virati*); the Śūdra is the cruel one (*krūra*). The Caṇḍāla’s house is the interior. The animal is *lālīka*; the *ḍākinī* is the sister. Fat is water; and in some places, "water" is said in the sense of "seize."

"Mudrā" refers to the limb-mudrā (*aṅgamudrā*). Its mention here on the occasion of the verbal code (*vākcchomma*) is for the purpose of indicating that the verbal and limb mudrās must be practiced in their fixed sequence; this applies likewise in subsequent sections. The touching of the teeth with the tongue indicates hunger. Thirst is "dwelling in fragrance" (*gandhavāsinī*); there is an alternative reading, *gandhavāhinī*. From where does it come? From such-and-such a place. "Showering flowers" (*puṣpakiraṇī*). A slight hanging down (*darolamba*). Laughter is the teeth. Rain is obstruction. Satisfaction is communication. Outside is "the one who bears the burden" (*dhuryuḥ*).

Clouds are fond of smoke; mountains have ridges; rivers are streams. A limb is a finger; in some places there is the recitation of fingers. The face is the mouth; the tongue is black mustard. Teeth are eaters; a banner is a row. A garland is a meter; wind is moving. An animal is the lord of beasts; time is a circle. "They go" is said in some places. A crossroads is level; a person is like the month of Phālguna. A great animal is a great syllable; *cchāgala* is *cchā*; a man is *nā*.

*Balīvarda* means a bull (*go*). *Mahiṣa* means a buffalo (*ma*). *Bhakṣaṇa* means eating (*bhā*). And *hā*: the word *hā* is feminine (*strīliṅga*), according to the statement, "by the power of *hā*. Even the servants at the feet of kings are *apyaka*; the word *apyaka* is feminine, according to the statement, "she is indicated in the *apyakā*. *Sthiti* means standing (*stha*). Touching the face with the hand indicates that one has eaten; touching the teeth indicates satisfaction (*tṛpti*); and *hom* also indicates satisfaction. *Lajjā* means shame (*hrīkā*). *Śūnya* and *kha* mean the female organ (*strīndriya*).

By touching him, she indicates: "Engage in sexual intercourse. By touching the thighs, she says: "I will do so by standing below. In some recensions, the reading at the touch of the thighs is "above" (*ūrdhvam*) instead of "below" (*adhastāt*). Even in the absence of the reading "above," the meaning remains the same: "I shall engage in sexual intercourse while standing above, and you shall stand below."
The thirteenth mañjarī in the Āmnāyamañjarī, the commentary on the Śrīsampuṭa.
